passages.section: Common Tasks and Navigation Guide from Chapter Leader Portal > Task: Report Chapter Events
passages.text:
Typical Process
Chapter Websites Hosted on Engage
Current and accurate chapter websites are a key component to communicating benefits, programs, events, and other important information to current and prospective members.
ISACA offers free website hosting to all chapters as microsites of the global Engage portal. Chapters are not required to use the Engage chapter website, but it offers myriad tools and services to help communicate your chapter’s great work. ISACA Global strongly recommends chapters take advantage of this free tool.
Note: Chapters that choose not to utilize their Engage website still must enter their events into Event Manager on Engage for chapter compliance.
Benefits of Engage-hosted chapter websites include:
Email Communication Tool – Allows you to easily disseminate information to your chapter members via email from the chapter website.

passages.section: Common Tasks and Navigation Guide from Chapter Leader Portal > Task: Report Chapter Events
passages.text:
Event Manager – This Engage event registration tool and calendar allows you to create and manage a variety of event types for your chapter, from online webinars to large, multi-day conferences with numerous registration options and sessions. Adding chapter events into Event Manager will also display them on the Global Events Calendar on Engage, with tags to help publicize your chapter’s event to a broader audience and categorize events by region.
Chapter Library – Use this central location to upload presentations, documents, articles, or other important information relevant to chapter members. All members of your chapter have access.
Member Directory – Connect and network with other IT professionals from your chapter. (Privacy settings enable searchability once a user has logged into Engage and can be managed from their Engage profile at any time.)

passages.section: Common Tasks and Navigation Guide from Chapter Leader Portal > Task: Report Chapter Events
passages.text:
Cross-site Configuration – ISACA Global, Engage, and your chapter website are all linked (i.e., “talk to each other”), which allows for a personalized experience when you log into Engage/your chapter website and cross publication of chapter events.
Job Board Code– Chapters will receive a unique code to share with local employers to post on ISACA’s Job Board for free. The job board postings are managed by ISACA’s Career Center vendor, taking the administrative burden off chapters to edit, manage, or expire old posts on their website.
Globally Managed Assets – The administrative burden is reduced by having ISACA Global services and initiatives automatically displayed on certain chapter website pages.
Community Slideshow – Chapters can easily display photos from chapter events and programs to showcase the member experience and your chapter’s services.

passages.section: Common Tasks and Navigation Guide from Chapter Leader Portal > Task: Report Chapter Events
passages.text:
Upgraded Site Design – The modern, streamlined design and navigation aligns with the ISACA Global Brand. Iconography is available to further assist with design.
Exclusive member-only pages – Create member-only content on your chapter website.

passages.section: Task: Access Compliance Information > Typical Process
passages.text:
Compliance
Annual Chapter Compliance Reporting: 1 November and 31 December.
Each year, chapters confirm that they meet 11 governance, financial, and operational requirements. The compliance process helps protect your chapter, supports strong governance, and maintains your chapter's affiliation with ISACA.
Submit your chapter's compliance report between 1 November and 31 December.
Compliance LIVE Webinar
Join the Compliance LIVE Webinar on 13 October at 10:00 am CT for key updates, practical tips, and answers to common questions.
Register Now
Compliance Support Sessions
Join a monthly Compliance Support Session for live Q&A and guidance on your compliance application, documentation, evidence, and OpenWater submission.
Fill out form to Register: 2026 Compliance Support Sessions
How to Complete Your Submission
Review the compliance rubric and all 11 requirements.

passages.section: Task: Access Compliance Information > Typical Process
passages.text:
Confirm whether your chapter meets each requirement.
Gather supporting documentation using the rubrics evidence examples.
Contact ISACA before the deadline if you need assistance.
Submit your Compliance Documentation
Compliance Requirements
The Compliance Rubric explains each requirement and includes examples of acceptable supporting documentation. Use it as your primary reference when completing the annual compliance review.
Access the 2026 Compliance Rubric
Reduce Year-End Work
Successful compliance begins long before the application is due. Boards should plan early, maintain records throughout the year, monitor progress regularly, and submit using organized, current evidence.
Suggested Timeline
Q1: Governance Documentation 
Plan early by confirming responsibilities and maintaining governance records.
Q2: Bylaws and Privacy Review 
Review key policies and update documentation as needed.

passages.section: Task: Access Compliance Information > Typical Process
passages.text:
Q3: Event Reporting and Audit Preparation 
Maintain event and financial records to support the year-end financial audit.
Q4: Audit Completion and Compliance Submission 
Finalize the audit and submit your compliance application.
Frequently Misunderstood Requirements
Bylaws Review 
Submitting bylaws alone does not demonstrate compliance. Chapters should document that the board reviewed the bylaws during the year in their meeting minutes, which should be available to ISACA Global for review if requested.
Financial Reporting 
Submit the most recent qualifying financial review, audit, approved compilation (with full written approval from ISACA Global for the current year), or verification document. Local legal requirements take precedence when they are more restrictive. More information and link to template are on the rubric.
Educational Events

passages.section: Task: Access Compliance Information > Typical Process
passages.text:
Chapters must conduct at least four educational events and post them on Engage and/or your chapter website. Past events may be added if needed. Please share links in the submission form to indicate where this information can be found.
Privacy Policy 
Review your privacy policy periodically to ensure it remains accurate and aligned with local requirements.
Need Help?
Contact ISACA Support before the Compliance deadline if:
You may not meet a compliance requirement.
You are unsure what compliance evidence is acceptable.
Local laws affect compliance.
You need to discuss available options.
Early communication creates the best opportunity to resolve issues and provide clarity.

This document provides an overview of the primary systems and tools used by ISACA chapter leaders. It is intended to help users understand where information and activities are managed across ISACA's chapter ecosystem. It does not include access-controlled information, member data, or direct system access instructions.

The Chapter Leader Portal serves as the primary operational resource center for ISACA chapter leaders. It provides access to chapter management tools, compliance resources, reports, forms, guidance, and chapter administration functions. Chapter leaders use the portal to support the governance and operation of their chapter.

- Access chapter compliance resources
- Review chapter reporting requirements
- Access chapter management tools
- Submit or support chapter administrative processes
- Access chapter forms and guidance
- Verify chapter membership status when authorized
- Access chapter-related reports and operational resources

C360 (Chapter 360) is ISACA's chapter enablement and management framework designed to support volunteer chapter leaders in operating effective, sustainable chapters. It helps leaders understand chapter operations, governance practices, and organizational maturity across key areas of chapter management.

- View chapter operational information
- Monitor chapter health and performance indicators
- Support governance and planning activities
- Review chapter maturity and operational practices
- Support leadership decision-making
- Access chapter-related metrics and organizational information

Engage is ISACA's online community and collaboration platform. It enables chapter leaders, volunteers, and members to connect, communicate, share knowledge, manage chapter websites, and support chapter activities.

- Participate in chapter leader communities
- Collaborate with other chapter leaders worldwide
- Access community discussions and resources
- Manage ISACA-hosted chapter websites
- Manage chapter events through Event Manager
- Access training materials and support resources
ISACA chapters use several reporting and submission tools to support operational and compliance requirements.

passages.section: Chapter Reporting Tools > Chapter Compliance Reporting
passages.text: Used to submit annual chapter compliance information and demonstrate adherence to the requirements of the Chapter Affiliation Agreement. Compliance reports are submitted annually through designated reporting systems.
Used to record chapter educational events and maintain chapter activity records. Event reporting supports chapter compliance requirements and member engagement tracking.

passages.section: Chapter Reporting Tools > CPE Upload Tool
passages.text: Allows chapter leaders to upload continuing professional education (CPE) attendance information for chapter event participants. This helps members receive appropriate educational credit for participation in chapter events.

passages.section: Chapter Reporting Tools > Board and Leader Roster Management
passages.text: Supports the maintenance and updating of chapter leadership records and authorized chapter contacts.

Chapter Leader Portal
- Operational hub for chapter leaders
- Access point for tools, forms, reports, and governance resources
C360
- Chapter management, performance, and enablement information
- Supports chapter oversight and planning
Engage
- Community, collaboration, websites, and event management
- Supports communication and member engagement
Reporting Tools
- Event reporting
- CPE reporting
- Administrative submissions
Together, these systems support chapter governance, operations, compliance, leadership collaboration, member engagement, and reporting activities across the ISACA chapter ecosystem.

Welcome!
Congratulations, and welcome to your role as the chapter president of your ISACA chapter!
The chapter president serves as the chief elected officer of the chapter and the primary local representative of ISACA. As the leader of the chapter’s board and volunteer organization, the president provides strategic direction, fosters effective governance, and supports the achievement of the chapter’s mission and objectives.
Working collaboratively with the board, volunteers, and staff (where applicable), the President helps ensure that chapter’s programs, services, and operations deliver value to members, promote professional growth and engagement and contribute to the chapter’s long-term sustainability and success.

The Chapter President is responsible for implementing the policies and decisions of the chapter board by:
• Ensuring the chapter operates in accordance with its bylaws, board-approved policies, and applicable ISACA Global requirements, and
• Exercising appropriate leadership and judgment to address operational matters when specific policies or procedures have not been established, while remaining accountable to the chapter board.
Additionally, the Chapter President should:
• Lead the chapter’s annual strategic planning process, working with the chapter board to establish goals and objectives that support member value, chapter sustainability, and alignment with ISACA’s global mission and strategic priorities.

• Monitor chapter performance and compliance with applicable ISACA Global and chapter requirements. If the chapter experiences challenges meeting established standards, the President should promptly engage the Chapter Experience team through ISACA Support for guidance and assistance.
• Provide leadership and oversight to the chapter board and volunteer leadership structure, ensuring effective coordination among officers, directors, committee chairs, and other volunteers in support of the chapter’s strategic goals.
Foster collaboration, accountability, and succession planning within the chapter’s leadership team to promote continuity and long-term success.
Roles and Responsibilities of the Chapter
President
Regional Strategic Advisory Council

All chapter presidents are ex-officio members of ISACA’s Regional Strategic Advisory Council (SAC). The SAC provides a forum for chapter leaders to share insights, identify regional needs and opportunities, and inform the development of initiatives that support members, chapters, and the profession. Participation in the SAC helps ensure that chapter perspectives are represented in regional discussions and strategic planning efforts.
Chapter Presidents will receive an invitation when meetings for their respective Regional SAC are scheduled and are encouraged to actively participate in these discussions.
Governance

As an independent legal entity, the chapter is solely responsible for its own legal, financial, and operational affairs. As Chapter President, you play a key role in helping ensure the chapter operates in accordance with applicable laws and regulations, the ISACA Chapter Affiliation Agreement, chapter bylaws and other ISACA Global policies and requirements.
To support effective governance, the Chapter President should:
• Promote compliance with applicable laws, regulations, chapter governing documents, and ISACA requirements.
• Help safeguard member and chapter data by supporting compliance with data privacy and security requirements, including applicable local regulations (such as GDPR) and ISACA policies.
•

• Lead the development and periodic review of the chapter's strategic plan in collaboration with the board, and monitor progress toward established goals and objectives.
• Implement the policies and decisions of the chapter board and support accountability for their execution.
• Exercise appropriate executive leadership and judgment on operational matters when specific policies or procedures do not exist, while remaining accountable to the chapter board.
• Recommend the establishment of committees and, with board approval and in accordance with the chapter bylaws, appoint committee chairs and other volunteer leaders as needed.
• Serve as an ex officio member of all committees, except the Nominating Committee, unless otherwise provided in the chapter bylaws.

• Oversee the nomination and election processes to help ensure compliance with the chapter bylaws and applicable governance requirements.
• Work with the board and volunteer leaders to identify risks to achieving strategic objectives and implement appropriate corrective actions when necessary.
• Ensure the chapter offers a sustainable portfolio of programs, events, and services that provide value to members and support member engagement, professional development, and chapter growth.
General Leadership

While the Chapter President provides leadership and oversight, responsibility for governance and strategic direction rests with the chapter board collectively. The President should work collaboratively with the board, committees, volunteers, and staff to advance the chapter's mission and long-term sustainability.
The Chapter President should:
• Provide leadership in developing and maintaining an effective chapter governance structure, including board and committee roles, responsibilities, and reporting relationships, in accordance with the chapter bylaws.
• Foster clear communication, accountability, and collaboration among board members, committee leaders, and volunteers.

• Inspire, support, recognize, and encourage board members, committee leaders, and volunteers to advance the chapter's mission and strategic objectives.
• Promote a culture of teamwork, inclusion, professionalism, and volunteer engagement throughout the chapter.
• Mentor and support officers, directors, committee chairs, and emerging leaders to strengthen leadership development and succession planning.
• Lead and facilitate the chapter's annual strategic planning process, working with the board to establish goals, objectives, priorities, and measures of success.
• Work with the board and volunteer leaders to establish an annual operating calendar that supports timely execution of key chapter activities, governance requirements, and strategic initiatives.

• Oversee periodic reviews of the chapter bylaws and governing documents and recommend updates, as appropriate, to ensure continued relevance and compliance.
• Provide oversight of chapter programs, events, communications, and marketing activities to help ensure alignment with the chapter's strategic goals, brand standards, and member needs.
• Provide oversight of the chapter's digital presence, including the chapter website and social media channels, to help ensure content is accurate, current, and consistent with ISACA and chapter policies.
• Supervise and support chapter staff, if any, in accordance with applicable employment policies and board direction.

• Lead succession planning efforts for chapter leadership positions by identifying, developing, and encouraging future leaders and volunteers in collaboration with the board and committee leaders.
• Serve as the chapter's primary ambassador and relationship builder, fostering collaboration with other professional organizations, community stakeholders, ISACA chapters, and regional leaders where appropriate.
• Support membership growth, retention, and engagement efforts by working with the Membership Director and other volunteers to develop and implement initiatives that deliver value to members and recognize member contributions and achievements.
Finances

The Chapter President shares responsibility with the chapter board for fiduciary oversight of the chapter and should work closely with the Chapter Treasurer to promote sound financial management, transparency, and compliance. While the Treasurer typically oversees the day-to-day administration of financial activities, the President helps ensure appropriate financial controls, reporting, and governance practices are in place.
The Chapter President should:
• Work with the Chapter Treasurer and board to help ensure compliance with applicable financial, labor, tax, and regulatory requirements.
• Promote effective risk management and strong internal controls over chapter finances.

o It is strongly recommended that chapters require dual authorization or multiple signatures for disbursements exceeding a board-established threshold and periodically review authorized signatories on all financial accounts.
o It is strongly recommended that the Chapter President and/or Treasurer regularly consult with the chapter's financial institution and financial advisors, as appropriate, to assess and implement fraud prevention and risk mitigation measures.
• Provide oversight of the chapter's budgeting, financial reporting, and financial management processes to help ensure compliance with chapter policies, applicable requirements, and generally accepted financial management practices.

• Review periodic financial reports and bank reconciliations with the Treasurer and ensure that material discrepancies, unusual transactions, or control concerns are promptly investigated and addressed.
• Help ensure that adequate financial records and supporting documentation are maintained in accordance with the chapter's record retention policies and applicable legal and regulatory requirements.
• Support the implementation and periodic review of a records retention policy. (An example Record Retention Policy is included in the appendix of the Chapter Treasurer Guidebook.)
• Ensure the board receives regular financial reports that accurately present chapter revenues, expenses, assets, liabilities, and budget performance using the chapter's established accounting structure.

• Encourage timely financial reporting and board review. Delays in producing financial information may indicate operational or control issues and can limit the board's ability to monitor financial performance, manage reserves, and take corrective action when necessary.
• Work with the Treasurer and board to address identified financial risks, budget variances, reserve shortfalls, or control deficiencies in a timely manner.
Effective financial stewardship is a shared responsibility of the chapter board. The President should work collaboratively with the Treasurer and other board members to promote accountability, transparency, and the long-term financial sustainability of the chapter.
Reporting

The Chapter President serves as the primary liaison between the chapter and ISACA Global and helps ensure timely, accurate, and transparent reporting to both ISACA and chapter stakeholders.
The Chapter President should:
• Serve as the primary point of contact with ISACA Global for the submission of required chapter information, board rosters, reports, inquiries, and other official communications.
• Work with the chapter board and applicable officers to ensure compliance with all annual reporting requirements and deadlines established by ISACA.

o This includes ensuring chapter events are entered into the Engage platform, required annual checklists are completed, and audit reports or financial verification letters are submitted within required timeframes following the chapter's Annual General Meeting (AGM).
o Coordinate the assignment, preparation, review, approval, and submission of required reports and supporting documentation to ISACA Global.
• Establish and support effective reporting processes that provide the board with timely information regarding chapter operations, strategic initiatives, membership trends, program performance, and financial health.
• Ensure the board receives regular reports necessary to fulfill its governance, oversight, and fiduciary responsibilities.

• Promote transparent communication with chapter members by providing regular updates on chapter activities, achievements, strategic priorities, and financial condition, as appropriate.
• Work with chapter officers, committee leaders, and volunteers to ensure reporting is accurate, complete, and submitted in a timely manner.
• Promptly communicate significant chapter issues, risks, compliance concerns, or operational challenges to the chapter board and ISACA Global, as appropriate.
Effective reporting supports transparency, accountability, informed decision-making, and the chapter's ongoing compliance with both ISACA requirements and sound association governance practices.
Meetings

The Chapter President is responsible for providing leadership during board and membership meetings and helping ensure meetings are effective, productive, and aligned with the chapter's strategic objectives. The President should preside over chapter and board meetings whenever possible. If the President is unable to attend, the Vice President or other designated officer should serve in that capacity in accordance with the chapter bylaws.
The Chapter President should:
• Work with the Chapter Secretary and other appropriate officers to develop agendas for board and membership meetings that focus on strategic priorities, governance responsibilities, and key operational matters.

• Collaborate with the Chapter Treasurer to review proposed budgets, financial reports, and significant financial matters before presentation to the board.
• Preside over regular and special meetings of the chapter and its board in accordance with the chapter bylaws and applicable governance requirements.
• Facilitate constructive discussion, encourage participation, and promote informed decision-making by the board.
• Help ensure meeting agendas, materials, and supporting information are distributed in advance to enable effective board deliberation and oversight.
• Maintain order during meetings and help ensure board business is conducted fairly, efficiently, and in accordance with the chapter's governing documents and adopted parliamentary procedures, if applicable.

• Ensure decisions, action items, and follow-up responsibilities are clearly identified and appropriately documented.
• Encourage active engagement by directors, officers, committee chairs, and other participants to support effective governance and leadership.
• Effective meetings enable the board to fulfill its governance responsibilities, make informed decisions, and advance the chapter's mission, strategic goals, and long-term sustainability.
Chapter Board Meetings
As required by the chapter bylaws, the chapter board should meet regularly throughout the year, with a minimum of four board meetings annually. The Chapter President should typically chair these meetings and help ensure they are conducted effectively and in accordance with the chapter's governing documents.

The Chapter President should be responsible for:
• Ensuring board meetings are conducted in compliance with the chapter bylaws, applicable policies, and established governance practices.
• Presiding over board meetings and facilitating productive discussion, informed decision-making, and appropriate board oversight.
• Recognizing, presenting, and ruling on motions in accordance with the chapter's adopted meeting procedures and parliamentary authority, if applicable.
• Helping ensure that all directors have an opportunity to participate in discussions and deliberations.
• Maintaining order and ensuring meetings are conducted efficiently and professionally.
• Confirming that board decisions, motions, and action items are clearly documented by the Secretary.

• Working with the board and Secretary to establish the date, time, and format of future meetings and communicate meeting schedules to board members in a timely manner.
• Monitoring follow-up actions arising from board meetings and supporting accountability for the completion of assigned tasks.
• Effective board meetings are essential to fulfilling the board's governance responsibilities, overseeing chapter operations, and advancing the chapter's strategic objectives.
Regular or Special Membership Meetings

As required by the chapter bylaws, the chapter should hold membership meetings as specified in its governing documents. The Chapter President should typically preside over these meetings and help ensure they are conducted in a manner that promotes transparency, member engagement, and effective governance.
The Chapter President should:
• Ensure membership meetings are conducted in accordance with the chapter bylaws, applicable policies, and established governance practices.
• Preside over regular, annual, and special membership meetings, as applicable.
• Facilitate orderly and productive discussions while encouraging member participation and engagement.

• Recognize, present, and rule on motions in accordance with the chapter's adopted meeting procedures and parliamentary authority, if applicable.
• Maintain order and ensure business is conducted fairly, professionally, and efficiently.
• Ensure members are provided with appropriate information regarding chapter activities, strategic priorities, governance matters, and financial performance, as appropriate.
• Work with the Chapter Secretary to ensure meeting proceedings, decisions, and actions are accurately documented.
• Coordinate with the board and chapter leadership to schedule and communicate membership meetings in accordance with bylaw requirements and notice provisions.

The Chapter President's responsibilities for membership meetings are generally consistent with those described under Chapter Board Meetings, with an additional emphasis on member communication, engagement, and transparency. Membership meetings provide an important opportunity to inform members, gather feedback, and strengthen the connection between the chapter's leadership and its membership.
Immediately Following the Annual General Meeting
Leadership Transition and Reporting

Following the chapter's Annual General Meeting (AGM), or whenever a change in leadership occurs, the outgoing Chapter President should promptly notify the Chapter Experience team through ISACA Support of all newly elected and appointed chapter leaders. This helps ensure chapter records remain accurate and that new leaders receive timely access to chapter resources, communications, systems, and support.
The outgoing Chapter President should also:
• Ensure that chapter officer and board member information is updated in accordance with ISACA requirements.
• Facilitate a timely and effective leadership transition by transferring relevant records, documentation, credentials, and institutional knowledge to incoming leaders.

passages.section: The outgoing Chapter President should also:
passages.text:
• Work with incoming officers to ensure continuity of chapter operations, governance activities, and strategic initiatives.
• Confirm that banking, financial, legal, and administrative records are updated as necessary to reflect leadership changes.
• Support the onboarding of new leaders and encourage their participation in available ISACA training, resources, and leadership development opportunities.
Chapter Leader Listing on Hosted Chapter Websites
Chapter site administrators are responsible for managing the content displayed on the chapter's About Us page within chapter websites hosted on ISACA Engage. Each chapter may determine the approach that best fits its needs, while considering member privacy, ease of maintenance, and the desired level of visibility for chapter leaders.

passages.section: Chapter Leader Listing on Hosted Chapter Websites
passages.text:
Options for displaying chapter leadership information include:
• Manually maintain leadership information by entering and updating board and committee leader details as changes occur. This option provides the greatest flexibility and control over content, format, and display. Example: Milwaukee Chapter.
• Display limited information and provide a general chapter contact method rather than listing individual leaders. This approach may be preferred by chapters seeking to minimize maintenance requirements or limit the public display of personal information.
Example: San Francisco Chapter.

passages.section: Chapter Leader Listing on Hosted Chapter Websites
passages.text:
• Publish a static board or leadership image that includes names, titles, and photographs. While this approach allows greater control over presentation, updates must be made manually and leader profiles will not be linked. Example: Sydney Chapter.
• Use the Engage leadership widget to dynamically display chapter leaders based on information maintained in ISACA's chapter leadership records. This option reduces manual maintenance because updates are reflected when ISACA Global updates the chapter's official leader roster. However:
o The display order cannot be customized.
o Individuals must upload their own photo to their Engage profile if they wish their photo to appear.

passages.section: Chapter Leader Listing on Hosted Chapter Websites
passages.text:
o Individuals must set their profile visibility to Public for profile information and photos to be displayed. Example: Malta Chapter.
Chapter leaders should periodically review their chapter's public website content to ensure information is accurate, current, and consistent with chapter preferences, privacy considerations, and ISACA requirements.
Need help with your chapter’s Engage site? Send an email to chaptersiteadmins@isaca.org.
Mentoring
The Chapter President and Vice President should actively support the development, engagement, and success of chapter volunteers. Providing guidance, coaching, and leadership development opportunities helps strengthen volunteer effectiveness, build future leaders, and support the long- term sustainability of the chapter.
The Chapter President should:

• Encourage and support the professional growth and development of chapter volunteers, committee members, and emerging leaders.
• Work with the Vice President, board members, and committee chairs to provide orientation, mentoring, coaching, and ongoing support to volunteers, as appropriate.
• Monitor volunteer engagement and performance and provide constructive feedback when expectations, responsibilities, or commitments are not being met.
• Address performance concerns in a timely and professional manner through coaching, mentoring, role clarification, or other appropriate support measures.
• Collaborate with board members and committee leaders to identify and develop future chapter leaders and promote leadership succession planning.

• Foster a positive volunteer experience that encourages continued engagement, leadership development, and knowledge transfer.
Succession Planning
Chapters are encouraged to establish leadership development and succession planning practices that help ensure continuity of operations and governance.
One approach is to create a President-Elect, Deputy Director, or similar leadership development position that allows an emerging leader to gain experience and prepare for future service as Chapter President.
Such positions can provide:
• A structured transition and leadership development period for future chapter leaders.
• Opportunities for mentoring and knowledge transfer from current leaders.
• Greater leadership continuity and organizational resilience.

• Enhanced volunteer engagement and leadership pipeline development.
If a chapter chooses to establish a President-Elect, Deputy Director, or similar position, the role, responsibilities, authority, and succession provisions should be clearly defined in the chapter's bylaws.
Turnover Procedures
Leadership Transition and Handover
A well-planned leadership transition helps maintain operational continuity, preserve institutional knowledge, and position the chapter for future success. The outgoing Chapter President should work closely with incoming leaders, officers, directors, committee chairs, and volunteers to ensure a timely and effective transfer of responsibilities.
As part of the leadership transition process, the outgoing Chapter President should:

• Ensure the timely transfer of relevant chapter records, files, correspondence, credentials, and institutional knowledge to incoming officers, directors, committee chairs, and other authorized leaders.
• Confirm that all required annual reporting and compliance obligations have been completed or appropriately assigned, including any reports due to ISACA Global.
• Establish a transition timeline and target completion date for all turnover activities.
• Coordinate with chapter officers, directors, and committee chairs to review and update chapter procedures, forms, operational documentation, and governance records, as appropriate.
• Prepare, or coordinate the preparation of, a list of open items and ongoing activities requiring follow-up by incoming leaders. Examples may include:

o Outstanding invoices awaiting payment approval or processing.
o Venue, facility, or service contracts for upcoming chapter events.
o Speaker, instructor, sponsor, or vendor agreements for future programs.
o Strategic initiatives, projects, or operational matters that remain incomplete.
o Other commitments, obligations, or action items requiring continued attention.
• Facilitate transition meetings between outgoing and incoming leaders to support knowledge transfer, answer questions, and promote continuity. These meetings may be conducted individually or as a group, depending on the chapter's needs.
• Work with the Treasurer to review and update the chapter's inventory of assets, equipment, records, and other chapter property.

• Ensure that all chapter-owned property, records, and resources are appropriately transferred to authorized incoming leaders.
• Confirm that banking, financial, and other administrative accounts are updated as necessary to reflect leadership changes, including authorized signatories.
Chapters are encouraged to maintain multiple authorized signers and appropriate internal controls in accordance with board-approved policies.
• Ensure access to chapter mailboxes, post office boxes, technology platforms, websites, social media accounts, cloud storage, email systems, and other chapter resources is transferred to authorized incoming leaders and removed for outgoing leaders, as appropriate.

• Transfer current correspondence files and other important records to the incoming Chapter President, including materials, resources, and guidance provided by ISACA Global that may support future chapter operations.
Recognition and Appreciation
The outgoing Chapter President should also consider coordinating a volunteer Recognition activity or event to acknowledge and celebrate the contributions of board members, committee leaders, volunteers, and members whose efforts supported the chapter's success throughout the year.
Appendix
Timetable for Action
President’s Annual Checklist
• Ensure all chapter events are included on the Engage chapter website.
• Between 1 November – 31 December each year,
o Submit the online compliance checklist.

o Submit the audit or financial verification letter to ISACA Global.
o Submit any other mandatory items to ISACA Global as needed.
o Conduct an orientation for all incoming chapter leaders. Include:
• Mission and vision statements
• Organizational history
• Bylaws and policies
• Strategic plan
• Financial summaries
• Committee information
• Meeting processes
• Chapter Affiliation Agreement
o Submit the list of volunteers appointed and elected at the AGM to the Chapter Experience team via ISACA Support.
o Develop chapter goals and strategies for the new year via a strategic planning session.
o Ensure all volunteers have signed and submitted to the chapter’s secretary the Conflict of Interest Statement and the Willingness to Serve Agreement.
• Within 60 days of the AGM:

o Ensure the chapter’s goals and strategic plans are in progress.
• Within 210 days (approximately 7 months) of the AGM:
o Begin recruiting volunteers for the following year/term.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board Meeting Minutes
passages.text: Board meeting minutes are the official record of what the board decided. They let the next meeting pick up where the last one ended, show members and partners how decisions were made, help settle later disagreements about what was agreed, and keep the chapter's memory when leaders change. Because minutes can be used as an official record, they should be accurate, plain and brief.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board Meeting Minutes
passages.section: What to include in board meeting minutes
passages.text: Board meeting minutes should include the date, time and place; whether it was a regular or special meeting; who chaired it, which board members attended and who was absent; whether a quorum was present; whether the previous minutes were approved, with any corrections; each motion, who made and seconded it, and the result of the vote; decisions and actions agreed, with who will do them; items held over to a later meeting; and the time the meeting ended. Attach reports instead of copying them into the minutes.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board Meeting Minutes
passages.section: What to leave out of minutes
passages.text: Minutes record decisions, not a word-for-word account of the discussion. Leave out personal opinions and remarks about people, arguments between members, praise or criticism, details of legal advice, jargon nobody will understand later, and anything said in confidence. Use names mainly for who made and seconded motions. Summarize the main points of an important debate in a sentence or two.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board Meeting Minutes
passages.text: The secretary drafts the minutes soon after the meeting, checks them against the agenda, and sends the draft to the board so members can suggest corrections. The board approves the minutes, with any corrections, at the start of its next meeting. Once approved, the secretary signs them (some boards also ask the president to sign) and files them. Unsigned or unapproved minutes are only a draft.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board Meeting Minutes
passages.text: Keep all approved minutes, with their attachments, in one consistent place that the board can find, with a backup copy. Hand them over to the next secretary and president when leaders change, so the record isn't lost. Rules on how long minutes must be kept differ by country and by your bylaws; many boards simply keep them permanently.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board Meeting Minutes
passages.text: Common mistakes are not recording whether a quorum was present, describing decisions too vaguely to act on, including remarks that could embarrass the chapter, sending minutes out late or approving them late, missing signatures, and filing them in different places so they can't be found later.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board and Officer Roles
passages.section: What the board as a whole does
passages.text: A board's job is oversight and direction, not running day-to-day activities. Its main responsibilities are to keep the mission in view, plan and then check progress against the plan, make sure programs serve the mission, protect the chapter's money and assets through a budget and financial controls, recruit and develop good board members, and keep the chapter legally and ethically sound. Each board member also owes the chapter care (decide carefully and with good information), loyalty (put the chapter's interests ahead of their own) and faithfulness to the mission and the rules.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board and Officer Roles
passages.section: What every board member is expected to do
passages.text: Every board member should attend board meetings, read the agenda and materials before each meeting, serve on at least one committee or take on a special task, keep up with the chapter's activities and policies, follow the conflict of interest and confidentiality policies, help find future leaders, and speak well of the chapter. Board members share responsibility for board decisions, including ones they voted against, and should disagree respectfully in the meeting rather than outside it.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board and Officer Roles
passages.text: The president (or board chair) leads the board as a team. Typical duties are to plan the agenda and run board meetings, make sure every member can take part, appoint committee chairs and suggest committee members, help with new member orientation, act as the board's main spokesperson, lead a regular board self-assessment, and mentor the person who will take over. The president has the same single vote as other members; some presidents speak last so they don't steer the discussion.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board and Officer Roles
passages.text: The vice president (or vice chair) is the backup leader, so the board is never without someone to lead. Typical duties are to run meetings when the president is absent, take on special assignments from the president, share leadership tasks, and prepare to step into the president's role.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board and Officer Roles
passages.text: The secretary looks after the board's records. Typical duties are to send meeting notices, record attendance and whether a quorum was present, take or review the minutes and bring them to the next meeting for approval, keep board records, documents and contracts safe and in one place, and keep track of board members' terms. Any board member can take minutes if needed, but the secretary makes sure they are complete and filed.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board and Officer Roles
passages.text: The treasurer looks after the chapter's money on behalf of the board. Typical duties are to prepare or oversee the annual budget and present it for approval, make sure board members receive clear, timely financial reports, chair any finance committee, help the board understand the chapter's financial position, and work with whoever reviews or audits the accounts. A treasurer needs some understanding of basic accounting and financial statements.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Board and Officer Roles
passages.section: Terms, job descriptions and holding more than one role
passages.text: Written descriptions of each board role help everyone know what is expected, and give the board something to refer back to later. A role description usually covers the role's duties, who it reports to, the term dates, the expected time commitment, and the skills it needs. Many boards limit how many terms in a row a person can serve, and stagger terms so the whole board never changes at once. It is usually better for one person to hold only one officer role. Your chapter's bylaws set the actual terms and limits.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Committees and Task Forces
passages.section: Standing committees, ad hoc committees and task forces
passages.text: A standing committee handles ongoing work year after year, such as finance, membership, programs or nominations. An ad hoc committee is set up for one purpose, such as reviewing the bylaws or drafting a strategic plan, and closes when the job is done. A task force is short and focused on one problem, such as planning an event. An advisory group gives expert advice but has no decision-making power. Committees usually make recommendations; the full board makes the decision.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Committees and Task Forces
passages.section: How many committees a chapter needs
passages.text: Most boards need fewer standing committees than they think. Review the committees every year against the work the chapter actually needs to do: close committees with no real work, merge committees whose duties overlap, and use short task forces for one-off jobs. Committees are tools for the board's work, not ends in themselves.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Committees and Task Forces
passages.text: Write down what each committee is for and what skills it needs, and share that widely so volunteers can decide whether to join. Match people to committees by their skills, interests and available time, and aim for a mix of experienced members and newer people. Each board member should serve on at least one committee, and usually on no more than two. Committees can include chapter members who are not on the board, which is a good way to spot future board members.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Committees and Task Forces
passages.text: A committee chair turns the board's goals into a work plan and meeting agendas, runs the committee's meetings, follows up with members who miss meetings, makes sure notes are kept, and reports the committee's progress and recommendations to the board. Give every committee a written charge with its goals and deadlines, and review it every year or two.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Committees and Task Forces
passages.text: At the end of each year or project, ask whether each committee met its goals, used its members' time well and still needs to exist. Short check-ins at the end of meetings also help. Use what you learn to thank strong contributors and to invite them toward larger leadership roles.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Conflicts of Interest
passages.section: What a conflict of interest is
passages.text: A conflict of interest arises when a board member's personal interest could influence, or look as if it could influence, a decision they take part in. It isn't only about money: a family tie, a job with a supplier or sponsor, or a role in a competing organization can all create a conflict. Conflicts are normal, since board members have lives and careers outside the chapter. What matters is that they are disclosed and handled openly.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Conflicts of Interest
passages.section: What a conflict of interest policy should include
passages.text: A conflict of interest policy should say why it exists, ask every board member to agree to follow it, require each board member to fill in a written disclosure of their outside ties every year, keep those disclosures on file and up to date, explain what happens when a member has a conflict on a decision, and expect members to speak up when a new conflict comes up during a discussion.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Conflicts of Interest
passages.section: What to do when a board member has a conflict in a meeting
passages.text: When a board member has a conflict of interest on an item, they should declare it before the discussion starts, leave the room for that item and not vote, and the minutes should record that they declared the conflict and did not vote. Some boards let the member answer questions first and then step out. The chair names the conflict and asks the member to step aside. If a member forgets, the chair should give a gentle reminder; if a member disputes the conflict, the chair can pause the item until it is resolved.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Conflicts of Interest
passages.text: Talk about conflicts of interest when recruiting new board members, include the policy in orientation, and review the disclosures when planning each agenda so the chair can spot conflicts in advance. A board with a range of members is less likely to have one conflict dominate a decision. If a conflict is serious and lasting, the board should discuss whether the member can keep serving in that role.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Leadership Succession and Handover
passages.text: Chapter leadership changes regularly, and much of what a leader knows can leave with them. Planning for succession keeps the chapter running smoothly through each change, brings in fresh ideas, and stops leadership resting on the same few people year after year. The best time to start is early in a term, not just before it ends.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Leadership Succession and Handover
passages.section: Building a pipeline of future leaders
passages.text: Treat every active member as a possible future leader. Give promising volunteers growing responsibility, for example a committee role, then a committee chair, then a board seat. Offer training as they go, especially in finance and strategy. A year as treasurer or committee chair is good preparation for president. Ask the whole board what qualities the next leaders need, and invite nominations from every board member.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Leadership Succession and Handover
passages.section: Handing over to the next president
passages.text: Before a term ends, the outgoing president should mentor the incoming president, share the open items and upcoming deadlines, introduce key contacts, and pass on records such as minutes, financial information and passwords, following the chapter's procedures. Writing down what worked, what didn't and what is unfinished saves the next leader months of rediscovery.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Leadership Succession and Handover
passages.text: Many boards keep the immediate past president on the board for a year after their term. They remember why past decisions were made, can advise the new president, and help keep plans on track. Their role is to support and advise, not to keep leading. Past leaders can also help by recruiting the next group of volunteers.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Leadership Succession and Handover
passages.section: Stepping up as a new leader
passages.text: A new leader should spend the first months learning how the chapter really works: its habits, who holds knowledge and influence, and how decisions get made. Build relationships with fellow board members early, since they drive what the board can achieve. Be honest about your own gaps and ask for help with them. As president, part of the job is to encourage the next group of members to step up.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Orienting New Board Members
passages.text: A new board member should have an orientation, even if they have served on other boards before. Every board has its own habits, customs and unwritten rules, and few people pick up governance on their own. A good orientation shortens the learning curve, so new members contribute sooner, and it gives the whole board one shared picture of how it works. It is also the formal start of working relationships between new and returning members.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Orienting New Board Members
passages.section: What to cover in a new board member orientation
passages.text: An orientation for new board members should cover the chapter's mission and goals, the key issues the chapter faces right now, what is expected of each board member (time, meetings, committee work), the board meeting calendar, a contact list of the people they will work with, the board handbook, and the minutes of recent board meetings. Leave time at the end for questions. Spend the session on how to be a good board member and how this board works, more than on organizational detail.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Orienting New Board Members
passages.text: Give every new board member a board handbook, on paper or as a link. A useful handbook holds a welcome letter, the chapter's history, its mission and goals, the bylaws, recent financial information, the strategic plan, a description of each committee and who chairs it, the role of each board member, and key policies such as conflict of interest. Update the handbook before each orientation, so it reflects new programs and policy changes. New members should read it on their own time before the session, so the session can be used for discussion.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Orienting New Board Members
passages.text: The chapter president usually leads the orientation, supported by whoever handles board development, such as a governance or nominating committee. Invite returning board members too: they can present their area, act as mentors, and show newcomers the range of people on the board. Some boards bring in a neutral facilitator so that everyone feels free to speak. ISACA's Chapter Experience team can tell you what ISACA provides for new chapter leaders.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Orienting New Board Members
passages.text: There is no single right format. An orientation can be a few hours or spread over several short sessions, in person or online; a full-day event can overload people. Decide the goals and the agenda in advance. Keep the setting informal, mix short presentations with discussion and questions, and include some social time, since getting to know each other helps the board work as a team. Make clear that the board acts as a group: decisions are made together, not by any one member.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Orienting New Board Members
passages.text: Orientation is a start, not the whole job. Pair each new board member with an experienced member as a mentor for their first year. Treat their first regular board meeting as the start of their formal duties, and check in after a few months to see what is still unclear. Some boards ask each new member to sign a short statement of what is expected of them and keep it with the board's records.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Recruiting and Engaging Volunteers
passages.section: Finding new volunteers and board members
passages.text: The most effective way to recruit a volunteer is to ask them personally. Look at the skills and backgrounds the board already has, note the gaps, and look for people who fill them, at events, through committees and through members' networks. Explain to each candidate why their skills would help and what the role involves before they say yes. Keep a list of possible future leaders all year, not only at election time.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Recruiting and Engaging Volunteers
passages.section: Setting clear expectations for board members
passages.text: Agree on what the chapter expects of every board member and tell new and returning members the same thing, ideally in writing. Typical expectations are to attend meetings regularly, arrive having read the materials, take part in at least one committee, use personal and professional contacts to help the chapter, and raise disagreements respectfully in the meeting. When members have different ideas about their role, the board stops working as a team.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Recruiting and Engaging Volunteers
passages.text: Learn what motivates each volunteer and give them work that uses their skills and interests. Give volunteers one clear person to contact, tell them how much time a task needs, and respect their limits to avoid burnout. Pair newer volunteers with experienced ones so knowledge is passed on. Ask volunteers for feedback, and act on it, so they feel like partners rather than helpers. When someone steps down, ask what would have made the role better.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Recruiting and Engaging Volunteers
passages.text: Thank volunteers often and publicly, for example at chapter events, in newsletters or in the minutes. Small gestures, such as a certificate, a mention at the annual meeting or a personal note, build loyalty. Recognition also shows other members that volunteering is valued, and it helps move strong volunteers toward leadership roles.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Recruiting and Engaging Volunteers
passages.text: Make board effectiveness a regular topic, for example once a year during planning. A short self-assessment survey every year or two helps members see where the board is strong and where it needs work. Offer training on the topics members ask for, such as reading financial statements, running meetings, meeting rules, the bylaws and strategic planning, and keep past agendas, minutes and budgets in one place so everyone can find them.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Recruiting and Engaging Volunteers
passages.text: New members are more likely to stay when someone connects with them early. Contact each new member personally within their first month, ideally from a fellow volunteer rather than an automated message, and check in again around six months. Send a short series of welcome messages over the first 90 days, each focused on one way to get involved, and offer easy first steps such as a local meetup or an online session.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Reviewing Your Chapter Governance
passages.section: When to review how the board is set up
passages.text: Consider a review of the board's structure when the same problems keep coming back: members aren't engaged, decisions take too long, roles overlap, or the bylaws no longer match how the chapter actually works. Reviewing the bylaws every few years, through a short-term committee, keeps them up to date.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Reviewing Your Chapter Governance
passages.section: Agree on the problem before the solution
passages.text: Changes to how a board is set up work best when people first agree on what the problems are. Start by writing down what good governance should achieve for the chapter, then compare that with how things work today and list the gaps. Only then design options to close the gaps. Jumping straight to a solution, such as "we need a smaller board", tends to split people into camps.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Reviewing Your Chapter Governance
passages.text: A practical sequence is: form a small review group that includes past leaders and some critical voices; agree what the board should achieve; list the gaps; have the board approve the gaps; design and compare several options; share the preferred option with members and listen to their concerns; refine it; have the board approve it; update the bylaws to match; and plan the changeover so the chapter keeps running. Keep detailed procedures in board policies rather than in the bylaws, so they can be updated more easily.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Reviewing Your Chapter Governance
passages.section: Pitfalls to avoid in a governance review
passages.text: Allow enough time, since agreement builds slowly. Talk often with influential members, but don't circulate a proposal before it's ready. Remember that board members serve the whole chapter, not one group within it. Aim for a decision everyone can live with, rather than one everyone loves.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Reviewing Your Chapter Governance
passages.text: Setting the chapter's direction is the board's job. Set aside dedicated time for planning at least once a year, keep the plan short and adaptable, and review progress against it regularly, for example every quarter. Use the plan to decide which projects to take on and which to decline.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Running Effective Board Meetings
passages.text: Start the agenda by deciding what the board must accomplish at this meeting. Carry over unfinished business from the last meeting, ask board members for items and give them time to reply, put the most important items first, and mark which items need a vote. Next to each item, note who will lead it and roughly how long it should take. A common order is: call to order, approval of the last minutes, reports, unfinished business, new business, and adjournment.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Running Effective Board Meetings
passages.text: Send the agenda and supporting papers well before the meeting, ideally one to two weeks ahead and within any notice period in your bylaws, so members can read them and arrive ready to decide. Short summaries, charts and comparisons with earlier results are easier to read than long reports. Fixing the year's meeting dates in advance helps volunteers keep them free.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Running Effective Board Meetings
passages.text: A consent agenda groups routine items, such as approving the last minutes and accepting written reports, so the board can approve them together in one vote without discussion. Any member can ask to move an item off the consent agenda for discussion. This saves meeting time for real decisions and strategy instead of listening to reports read aloud.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Running Effective Board Meetings
passages.text: The person chairing the meeting, usually the president, should start and end on time, keep to the agenda, and gently stop discussions that wander. Make sure every member gets a chance to speak, draw out quieter members, and welcome different views before a decision. When an item can't be settled, it can be postponed or passed to a committee. If your bylaws adopt a set of meeting rules such as Robert's Rules of Order, the chair should know how motions and votes work under them.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Running Effective Board Meetings
passages.text: Within a day or two, send a short note of decisions and action items, with who will do what by when. Carry open action items onto the next agenda as unfinished business. The secretary should send the draft minutes soon after, while memories are fresh. Some boards take five minutes at the end of each meeting to ask what worked and what to change.

passages.document: Best Practice Guide: Running Effective Board Meetings
passages.text: The most common mistakes are putting too many items on one agenda, leaving too little time for difficult topics, burying the important items at the end, spending most of the meeting on reports instead of decisions, and ending without anyone assigned to follow up. Long meetings with no decisions are a common reason volunteers lose interest and leave a board.
